To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

maternal vitamin A intake during pregnancy and early life, as well as neonatal supplementation with vitamin A and retinoic acid in early postnatal life, differentially regulates chon-drocyte growth, aggrecan expression, and matrix metalloprotease 13 expression in neonatal femurs of rats.
maternal VA intake during gestation and lactation and neonatal VARA intake in early life alter neonatal bone development and chondrocellular gene expression in the femur.
maternal VA intake during lactation, as opposed to during pregnancy, and neonatal VARA intake in early life, can affect chondrocytes in the neonatal femur.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of perinatal exposure to VA on neonatal chondrocytes.
the effect of VA intake on skeletal development.
understanding how the maternal diet during pregnancy and lacta-tion and neonatal exposure to VARA influence neonatal bone development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

maternal VA intake and direct oral supplementation of VA + RA to neonates can differentially regulate chondrocytic growth and gene expression in the neonatal femur, and that the combination of maternal VA and VARA supplementation can alter the ratio of aggregan:MMP in the neonatal growth plate.
VA supplementation of the mother and/or the newborn is detrimental to bone development in the rat.
maternal VA intake and neonatal VARA exposure have a differential impact on the expression of genes involved in cartilage and bone development.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
maternal vitamin A (VA) supplementation in excess of the requirement for normal growth and development may be harmful for offspring bone growth and development.

maternal VA deficiency during gestation and lactation may have long-term effects on bone development and that the use of VA supplements during pregnancy and lactating should be considered with caution.
VA and RA are essential to skeletal development, but that excess VA and RA may have deleterious effects on bone development.
The main takeaway from our work is that
maternal VA intake and neonatal VARA intake may interact to affect neonatal skeletal development, which may have implications for bone development and growth in early life and later life.
the effects of maternal diet on offspring bone growth are mediated by the interaction between maternal and offspring vitamin A status, with the latter being more important than the former.
maternal VA intake and neonatal VARA can alter neonatal chondrocytes, but that the effects depend on the maternal diet and on the neonatal VARA dose.
